The reporter attributed the event to potential confusion between the assigned heading of 160 and altitude of 6,000, noting the aircraft remained clear of terrain.

ASRSN:2175874.n: In EWR while taxing (night time) to gate XX, cleared to taxi north on U then on Y then Taxiway 1 to gate. While establish and taxing north on U a small white pickup truck traveling west didn't stop clear of U (they were on the vehicle road that parallels Y). I told the CA to stop (he stated afterwards that he didnt see truck as it was coming from our right and he was getting ready to turn left). He was able to very quickly bring the aircraft to a stop. The pickup truck finally saw us and stopped immediately in front of us before reversing clear of U. If we had not stopped I feel we would have hit the pickup truck. Incident was immediately reported to Ramp who asked us to inform ops once we were at gate (CA did talk to Ops). A vehicle stopped in front of us while taxiing on the expanded north ramp. While taxiing west on taxiway A we were cleared by ramp control to turn right onto taxiway U, Y, then Taxiway 1 to our gate. After turning north on taxiway U and prior to taxiway Y a pickup truck drove from east to west, right to left, in front of us. The vehicle was on a service road. The first officer saw it first and called my attention to it. I had to stop somewhat abruptly to avoid a conflict. The vehicle got nearly directly in front of us before it stopped quickly and began backing up to its proper hold position. I estimate when we both stopped we were roughly 100 feet from each other. After the vehicle backed up we resumed our taxi to the gate. We reported the incident over the radio to the ramp controller and to operations after gate arrival per the ramp controller's request.
ASRSN:2175874.s: While taxiing at night at EWR, a pilot stopped the aircraft to avoid a white pickup truck that entered Taxiway U from a parallel service road. The truck stopped approximately 100 feet in front of the aircraft before reversing, preventing a collision.

ASRSN:2175875.n: I found the plane to have a very small change in force 3/4 through the right rudder input. It was not always felt on every push of the rudder. I looked at the back of the plane and the rudder seemed to very slightly catch on the throw to the right at about 80 to 90 percent through the rudder throw. I verified little to no wind. Mx (Maintenance) said they felt it too, but could not identify an underlying cause. I coordinated my findings with the Chief Pilot and Maintenance Control.I feel this was probably flyable, but I think that if I was standing in front of a bunch of FAA officials (in the event something happened), I would have a hard time justifying why I took an airplane that I felt was not 100%. This maybe capable of being flown by a flight test team to a repair location.In my professional opinion, the rudder issue is probably not anything big. It could be a pulley that needs lubed or some part of a PCU (Power Control Unit) that is wearing out. If I was a passenger, I would want a 100% plane which is why I chose to give it back to Mx instead of taking it.
ASRSN:2175875.s: The pilot reported a slight rudder catch at 80-90% right throw during preflight checks, which Maintenance also felt but could not diagnose. The pilot grounded the aircraft for further inspection, suspecting a pulley or Power Control Unit issue, rather than flying it to a repair location.

ASRSN:2175878.n: On departure we experienced ENG BLEED OFF L and PACK OFF L EICAS messages. After resetting the left bleed air switch in accordance with the checklist, the left bleed operation and pack were restored but the crew noticed the left bleed pressure was fluctuating abnormally. We contacted dispatch and requested a conference with Maintenance Control. After discussion with Maintenance Control, we decided to continue the flight and access the pressure fluctuations prior to entering ETOPS airspace. Unfortunately, the left bleed began to operate intermittently with increased pressure fluctuations and additional ENG BLEED OFF L messages. The Captain switched off the left engine bleed and left pack in accordance with the checklist and contacted dispatch and Maintenance Control. After a short discussion, the decision was made to execute an air return to ZZZ and land overweight. The arrival, approach and landing were uneventful.
ASRSN:2175878.s: The crew experienced fluctuating left bleed pressure and ENG BLEED OFF L messages during departure. After the condition worsened, they returned to ZZZ and landed overweight following a decision with Maintenance Control.

ASRSN:2175892.n: During our crew brief at JPX a taxi route was planned from the FBO ramp to runway 10 via F, runway 16-34, H and A. Neither our company feasibility notes nor company briefing charts on Jepp FD Pro contain any restriction-information regarding exiting the ramp via F in the fleet. This is a narrow taxiway and its taxiway sign height (given how narrow the taxiway is) will have reduced clearance to the inboard section of the long wing. The inboard section of this wing sits lower due to its dihedral angle causing a reduced clearance when using that taxiway. Once we got close to taxiway F and visually confirming on both sides we could proceed, we agreed there should be a note for our fleet to avoid using taxiway F.
ASRSN:2175892.s: The flight crew identified a potential wingtip clearance issue on narrow taxiway F at JPX due to the aircraft's dihedral angle and sign height. They concluded that company briefing charts should include a restriction to avoid this taxiway for their fleet.

ASRSN:2175974.n: On RNAV X 31 into KLGA. Ground PROX caution sounded while on GP. CA verbalized a 850fpm descent. While making the turn at Citi Field, the GPWS briefly blipped an obstacle warning, twice, with a few seconds pause between the blips. Aircraft was on the GP, no descent rate was was observed exceeding 850fpm, and no obstacles were observed within three GP or approach course. We continued to a normal landing. Use of the autopilot is always a good idea on this and similar approaches.
ASRSN:2175974.s: The crew flying an RNAV X 31 approach into KLGA experienced two brief GPWS obstacle warnings while turning at Citi Field. Despite the alerts, the descent rate remained under 850 fpm, no obstacles were observed, and the aircraft completed a normal landing.

ASRSN:2175985.n: We landed at ZZZ. We pulled into gate XX for parking. I set the parking brake, but the plane moved forward. The nosewheel was chocked and we shut off the engines. We completed the ECAM proceedure. We contacted OPS and MX. We had a Parking brake fault, brakes release ECAM. I made a logbook write up.
ASRSN:2175985.s: The pilot reported that after landing and parking at gate XX, the aircraft moved forward despite the parking brake being set and the nosewheel chocked. This resulted in a "Parking brake fault, brakes release" ECAM message, prompting engine shutdown, maintenance contact, and a logbook entry.

ASRSN:2175991.n: Cleared for RNAV X 31 into LGA, aircraft configured and stabilized IAW (In Accordance With) with company RNAV X 31 pages, aircraft configured at 1000ft stabilized. 500' aircraft configured and stabilized. It was unknown to the First Officer and myself that the aircraft was high on the approach until rollout to align the aircraft with the runway after the left hand turn base to final on the RNAV X 31 approach. The First Officer disconnected the autopilot around 1000' and continued the approach following the FMS without any lateral or vertical deviation. As the aircraft was maneuvered to align with Runway 31 it was noticed that we were high according to the PAPI. However, according to the FMS the aircraft was right on glide path. We were unsure of the issue at the moment, the First Officer disregarded the FMS glide path and decided to increase descent to align with the PAPI vertical path. When doing so the aircraft was in a consistent 1000' per minute descent briefly reaching 1200' FPM with an immediate correction back to 1000'. We both knew something was not right considering the discrepancy between the PAPI vertical glide path and the FMS vertical glide path. Unfortunately with the large left hand turn the PAPI are out of sight for a majority of the approach, decreasing our situational awareness of our actual glide path. The First Officer and I both were prepared to call for a go-around, however the aircraft was still within the stabilized approach criteria and given the visual conditions and the current descent rate it was in both of our judgement that a safe landing within the touchdown zone could be made. Not leaving out the possibility that a go around could still be called if the circumstances changed. The aircraft touched touchdown within the touchdown zone and a full stop was made without any further issues. The question still remained. What happened? Why did the FMS have a large discrepancy when compared to the PAPI? After parking the aircraft at the gate a long debrief commenced without a solid answer. It was not until retrieving a new ATIS that I noticed that the airport altimeter 30.21 and we had 30.10 set. It is still unknown where we received the altimeter setting of 30.10. My assumption is that when cleared to descend VIA the STAR that 30.10 may have been given, or when checking in with approach an altimeter setting given by the controller was misinterpreted by us or misread by the controller. Again these are assumptions and cannot conclude the actual reason for setting 30.10. A 30.10 setting did not seem unusual given that we began the day with an altimeter setting of 30.40+ and had been decreasing rapidly throughout the day. To further solidify the importance of a correct altimeter setting it is in my opinion that if this approach was conducted in IMC, once clear of clouds there would not be enough time to maintain a stabilized approach to land and an immediate go -around would be conducted.Suggestions:This is a valuable lesson learned when given an altimeter setting to double check it with the airport digital ATIS or ask for clarification from ATC if unsure.
ASRSN:2175991.s: The flight crew flew an RNAV X 31 approach into LGA and landed safely despite being high due to an incorrect altimeter setting of 30.10 instead of the correct 30.21. This discrepancy caused a conflict between the FMS glide path and PAPI indications, which was only identified after landing.
